summary: Over the last 4 weeks your training has been heavily cycling-biased with solid aerobic bike volume (multiple rides 60–225 min), but running is critically under-represented — only one run in the entire block, executed at a very high average HR of 169 bpm. Sleep is consistently short (most nights 230–415 min, well below the 7–8 h optimal), body battery remains low-to-moderate throughout, and the two recent days showing battery values of 0–2 are a clear fatigue red flag. With the Half Oceanman 5,000 m swim just 7 days away, the priority is to protect freshness and execute a confident taper, then use the following week to safely absorb the race before the Treviso 10K on Oct 10.
suggestions: Sleep is your biggest limiter right now — most nights are under 6 hours and body battery is chronically suppressed; aim for at least 7.5 hours tonight and every night through race week, as no training session can compensate for this level of sleep deficit before a 5 km open-water race.

Your sole run in 4 weeks was at 169 bpm average (likely near max), so do not attempt any quality running before the Treviso 10K — the shakeout jogs already planned at 7:00+/km and ≤130 bpm are exactly right; stick strictly to those targets and abort if HR climbs.

For the Half Oceanman 5,000 m swim, your open-water pace has been 28–31 min/km (roughly 2:50–3:10/100 m), which is slower than the 2:30/100 m target — factor a realistic 42–48 min finish for the 5 km and pace the first 1,500 m conservatively to avoid blowing up.

After the Half Oceanman on Oct 3, take at least 2 full rest days (Oct 4–5) before resuming any structured training — a 5 km open-water race is a significant physiological stress and you need those days to be truly fresh for the Treviso 10K eight days later.

From Week 17 onward, running intervals at 4:55–5:10/km are aggressive given your current running fitness; consider starting the first session at 5:20–5:30/km and only tightening pace once HR at that effort settles below 160 bpm.
